input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

output:
We compare our graph-aware pipeline against a single baseline designed to reflect a straightforward, widely used production strategy for long-form generation, and we evaluate systems using a combination of automated checks, structured human annotation, and targeted qualitative analysis. Below we describe the baseline and provide operational definitions for all primary metrics, the annotation and adjudication protocol, and the statistical and qualitative analysis plan used to compare methods.

Baseline comparator
- Linear prompting baseline: sections are generated in document order in a single forward pass. For parity with our method, the baseline uses the same language model family, the same evidence index, and identical resource budgets for retrieval; it differs only in (i) the absence of an explicit section dependency graph and leaf-first scheduling, and (ii) prompts that request full sections in sequence rather than JSON-constrained, evidence-first section outputs.
- Implementation note: both systems emit machine-readable JSON per section so that automated checks and human annotation operate on comparable artifacts.

Primary evaluation metrics (operational definitions)
- Citation coverage: for a generated section, the proportion of distinct factual assertions that are accompanied by at least one explicit, machine-parsable citation reference in the section JSON. This metric is computed automatically from the JSON field that lists assertion→citation mappings and is reported at the section and document level.
- Unsupported-assertion rate (hallucination rate): the fraction of asserted statements that human annotators mark as lacking adequate supporting evidence in the retrieval corpus. Annotation proceeds at the assertion level (see below) and the metric is the number of assertions adjudicated as unsupported divided by the total number of assertions examined.
- Reviewer-style quality scores: coarse human judgments on dimensions relevant to scientific writing, collected on pre-defined Likert scales (e.g., 1–5). Dimensions include: overall factual accuracy, adequacy of citations, local coherence, and global rhetorical flow. These scores are used to capture holistic quality aspects that are not fully measurable via automated checks.
- Edit burden (secondary, automated): a proxy for post-hoc correction cost computed as the number of atomic edits (insertions, deletions, substitutions) required to make a generated section pass automated validation checks and annotator corrections; derived from diffs between initial generated JSON and final curated JSON.

Annotation and adjudication protocol
- Assertion segmentation: annotators work on a per-assertion basis. A small tool displays the section JSON, the embedding of each assertion (text span), the explicit citations attached by the generator, and the top-ranked retrieved evidence items injected during generation.
- Annotation labels: for each assertion, annotators select one of: Supported (sufficient evidence in provided retrieval corpus and citations), Unsupported (no adequate evidence in corpus), or Ambiguous (evidence insufficiently specific or contradictory). Annotators may also mark a supporting-citation mismatch (citation present but not relevant to the assertion).
- Adjudication: each assertion is labeled independently by two annotators. Disagreements are resolved by a senior adjudicator who (a) reviews the assertion and provided evidence items, (b) consults additional retrieved material if needed, and (c) issues the final label. All adjudication decisions are logged with short rationales to support later error analysis.
- Coverage sampling: to balance annotation cost and coverage, we sample assertions stratified by section type (e.g., Methods, Results, Related Work) and by system; sampling ensures comparable representation across systems and domains.

Automated validation and pre-annotation checks
- Prior to human annotation, every generated section JSON is processed by automated validators that (a) verify JSON schema conformance, (b) extract assertion→citation mappings to compute initial citation coverage, and (c) flag obvious citation-format errors or missing required fields. These automated outputs are used to prioritize human review (e.g., sections with low automated citation coverage are oversampled for annotation).

Statistical analysis plan
- Per-metric reporting: for each metric we report descriptive statistics aggregated per-section and per-document (means and dispersion). Primary comparisons between graph-aware and baseline systems are performed at the section level using paired analyses, so that each section-topic pair serves as its own control.
- Inferential testing: we apply standard two-sided paired tests appropriate for the data distribution (nonparametric paired tests when assumptions of normality are not met) and report associated effect-size measures. We also correct for multiple comparisons where multiple related hypotheses are tested.
- Inter-annotator agreement: agreement on categorical labels (Supported/Unsupported/Ambiguous) is quantified using a standard reliability coefficient and is reported alongside metric results to contextualize annotation variability.
- Robustness checks: we run sensitivity analyses that vary sampling strata and rerun comparisons on subsets of sections (e.g., only Methods, only Related Work) to identify whether effects are concentrated in particular rhetorical roles.

Qualitative analysis and error taxonomy
- Representative examples: we present hand-selected examples for three error categories—(1) unsupported factual claims, (2) citation-mismatch errors (citation present but irrelevant), and (3) coherent but under-cited narrative claims. Examples include the generator output JSON, the retrieved evidence used at generation time, and annotator rationales.
- Error taxonomy: adjudication logs are analyzed to derive a small taxonomy of common failure modes; this taxonomy is used to inform targeted mitigations (e.g., stricter retrieval thresholds, prompt edits) and to guide future evaluations.
- Case studies: for a subset of documents we provide before/after comparisons that show how JSON-constrained editing and adjudication reduce unsupported assertions and facilitate correction.

Reporting and reproducibility
- All evaluation scripts, the exact JSON schema used for measurement, annotation instructions, and adjudication rubrics are archived with the project code release to support reproducibility of the reported comparisons. Where internal or restricted-source materials are used (see Limitations), we report evaluation outcomes separately and clearly mark which parts of the analysis rely on restricted data.

Limitations of the protocol
- The evaluation emphasizes citation fidelity and unsupported-assertion detection rather than broad external validity; we report results conservatively and qualify any claim about generalization to other domains or larger-scale settings. Detailed limitations and mitigation strategies are discussed in Section 6.2.
